---
title: "Performance and big data"
description: >
  What the compile-once design does and does not buy you, how datashade
  draws millions of points by aggregating before it draws anything, and how a
  widget keeps a million points hoverable.
---

```{r}
#| include: false
have_all <- all(vapply(
  c("vellum", "vellumplot", "vellumwidget"),
  requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE
))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%",
  eval = have_all
)
if (have_all) suppressMessages(library(vellumverse))
```

Two things make plotting slow at scale: solving the layout, and drawing one mark
per data point. This article is about the second, which is where the large wins
are, and it is honest about the first.

Moving the scene graph, layout, and rendering into a compiled engine helps, but it
is an ordinary constant-factor improvement, not the reason to choose this stack —
`grid` on a modern machine is not slow for a normal plot either. The change in
*kind* comes from `datashade()`: when the data has more points than the output has
pixels, it aggregates into an image before anything is drawn, so cost stops
tracking the row count altogether.

## Where the time goes, and doesn't

In a `grid`-based stack, a plot's display list is replayed on every resize, text
has to be measured against whatever device is current, and every unit in the tree
re-resolves each time. (Point marks themselves are not one grob per point:
`ggplot2` emits one `pointsGrob` with vectors, as it should. The per-point cost is
in the engine's draw loop and in whatever the device does with each symbol.)
`vellum` moves that work down into Rust: metrics are available at construction
time, layout is a single explicit pass, and one render walk emits the chosen
backend. The consequence for
performance is that the R-side cost of a plot is building the spec, which is
cheap; the drawing cost is paid once, in compiled code.

That handles moderately large plots well. But no amount of engine speed helps
if the plot asks the renderer to draw two million individual circles into an
SVG: the file alone would be enormous, and most of those marks would land on
the same pixel. That is the problem `datashade()` solves.

## datashade: aggregate, then draw

`datashade()` bins points into a grid the size of the output image, counts
how many land in each cell, and colours the cells by density. It returns a
single raster, one image, instead of millions of marks. The binning is a
one-pass aggregation in Rust, so the cost scales with the number of *pixels*,
not the number of *points*. Ten thousand points and ten million points cost
almost the same to draw, because the output is the same-sized image either
way.

### The grammar-level way

In `vellumplot`, `mark_datashade()` is a mark like any other. Here are a million
points, drawn as a density field:

```{r datashade-mark}
set.seed(1)
n <- 1e6
df <- data.frame(
  x = rnorm(n),
  y = rnorm(n) * 0.5 + rnorm(n)
)

vplot(df) |>
  mark_datashade(x = x, y = y)
```

`mark_datashade()` takes `width` and `height` (the aggregation grid, default
`400 × 300`), a `colors` ramp, and `how`, which controls how counts map to
colour. The default `how = "eq_hist"` equalises the histogram so that a few
very dense cells do not wash out the rest of the structure.

### The backend-level way

The same aggregation is available in `vellum` as `datashade()`,
which returns a `raster_grob` you place in a scene yourself. Use this when
you are building a bespoke visual rather than a grammar plot:

```{r datashade-vellum}
set.seed(1)
n <- 1e6
x <- rnorm(n)
y <- x * 0.5 + rnorm(n)

vl_scene(6, 4.5, bg = "white") |>
  push(vl_viewport(xscale = range(x), yscale = range(y))) |>
  draw(datashade(x, y, width = 450, height = 300,
                 colors = c("#fde0dd", "#7a0177")))
```

Because `datashade()` bins over `xlim × ylim` (defaulting to the data range),
you draw it inside a viewport whose `xscale`/`yscale` match those limits so
the image lines up with axes you add around it.

## Tuning the density mapping

`how` decides how cell counts become colour, and it is the knob that most
changes what you see:

- `"eq_hist"` (default): histogram equalisation; best for revealing
  structure across a wide range of densities.
- `"log"`: log of the count; a gentler compression than equalisation.
- `"cbrt"`: cube root; gentler still.
- `"linear"`: raw counts; only useful when density is fairly uniform.

`colors` is any vector of colours forming the ramp from sparse to dense, and
`weight` lets you accumulate a summed quantity per cell instead of a plain
count, a weighted density.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# emphasise the tails with log scaling, custom ramp
vplot(df) |>
  mark_datashade(x = x, y = y, how = "log",
                 colors = c("#f7fbff", "#08306b"))
```

## When to reach for it

The rule of thumb is the pixel count. If your scatter has more points than
the plot has pixels, tens of thousands and up, overplotting means most
marks are invisible anyway, and `datashade()` shows the density they were
hiding while rendering in constant time. Below that, a plain `mark_point()`
is fine and keeps every point individually addressable (which matters for
interactivity; a datashaded image is one raster, not a thousand hoverable
points).

## Interactive at scale

Datashading gives up the individual points. When you need them, hoverable and
selectable in a browser, `vellumwidget` keeps them without putting one SVG node
per point on the page. Above `raster_threshold` keyed marks (20,000 by
default), `as_widget()` switches to *raster mode*:

- The chrome (axes, gridlines, titles, legend, text) stays real SVG, so axes
  re-tick as you zoom.
- The marks arrive as one image, rendered by `vellum`, plus a compact index of
  every mark's key and box. Hover, click, brush and lasso hit-test against the
  index, so they work with no per-point DOM.
- Alongside it ships vellum's *display list*: each mark's exact geometry and
  paint, in paint order. Zoom in and the marks in view are redrawn exactly from
  it rather than magnified. A list of 50,000 marks or more is drawn with
  WebGL2 where the browser supports it (a million points redraw in about
  10 ms); gradients, dashed strokes and grouped marks stay on the 2D canvas.
  Zoom in far enough (fewer than 3,000 marks in view) and those marks become
  real SVG nodes again.

The display list is shipped for up to `max_marks` marks (2 million by
default, about 6 MB per million points). With the display list (up to
`max_marks`), conditions, `filter_by()`, legend hiding and crosstalk filters
show at every zoom; above it they show only once zoomed into the detail tier.
Above `max_marks` the widget falls back to the image plus a bounding-box index, and the plot usually reads better as a
density anyway, with `mark_datashade()` or `mark_hex()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
as_widget(p) # raster mode above 20,000 keyed marks

# move the switch, or ship a bigger display list
as_widget(p, render = render_options(raster_threshold = 50000))
as_widget(p, render = render_options(max_marks = 5e6))
```

vellumwidget's [big-data
article](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumwidget/articles/big-data.html)
describes the tiers, their settings and their fallbacks in full.

## Choosing an output format at scale

The format you render to interacts with data size. A raster target (`.png`)
is a fixed-size grid of pixels regardless of how much data went into it. A
vector target (`.svg`, `.pdf`) stores every mark as an element, so a
half-million-point scatter produces a half-million-element file, and a
`.pptx` slide holds one shape per mark. For large data, prefer raster output,
or datashade first so that even the vector output is a single embedded image.

The SVG writer keeps each element small: a circular point is a `<circle>`,
a filled, outlined shape is one element rather than two, transforms are baked
into the coordinates, and coordinates are rounded to 0.01 px, so a 5,000-point
keyed scatter is about half a megabyte. Animations encode their
GIF frames in parallel (palette quantisation and dithering run on the worker
threads that rasterise each frame), so a 150-frame, 1200 × 800 GIF takes a few
seconds rather than most of a minute; APNG is faster still. See [one scene, many
outputs](one-scene-many-outputs.html) for how the same spec reaches each
format.

## Diagnosing a slow or heavy scene

`vellum` ships a couple of tools for when a plot is larger or slower than you
expect:

```{r}
#| eval: false
why_size(s, "panel")    # a named node's resolved size, and what determined it
vl_clear_render_cache() # drop cached compile/raster state
```

For scenes with an expensive sub-tree that is drawn repeatedly, a viewport
can cache its rendered content with `vl_viewport(..., cache = TRUE)`, so the work
is done once and reused.

## Summary

- The engine (scene graph, layout, render) runs in compiled code, so the R-side
  cost of a plot is building the spec. Useful, but a constant factor.
- `datashade()` / `mark_datashade()` render arbitrarily many points in time
  proportional to the image size, by aggregating to a density raster before
  drawing.
- `how` and `colors` shape how density reads; `weight` gives weighted
  densities.
- In a widget, raster mode keeps up to `max_marks` points (2 million by
  default) hoverable, with an exact WebGL2 or canvas redraw as you zoom.
- For large data, prefer raster output or datashade before going to vector.
